The package gcTMB fits growth curves over time by maximum likelihood with the Template Model Builder (TMB). The curves can depend on covariates, have random effects for repeated measurements of the same individuals, and have autocorrelated residuals, and the response can follow a range of distributions. This overview shows most of the features in one document, with short examples; five vignettes go into each topic in depth:

1. *Growth models and their parameters* (`vignette("growth-models")`): the formulas of the growth models, the meaning of their parameters, inflection points and maximum growth rates, fitting and comparing the models, confidence intervals and simple treatment effects;
2. *Fixed and random effects* (`vignette("fixed-random-effects")`): covariates and random effects of the parameters, likelihood ratio and F-tests of their inclusion, and count data;
3. *Timing and maximum growth rates* (`vignette("timing-rates")`): `timeto()` and `maxrate()` with treatment and genotype effects, the maximum growth rate as a parameter, and pairwise comparisons;
4. *Correlation structures* (`vignette("correlation")`): temporal correlation of the residuals within individuals over time, and spatial correlation between neighbouring trees, with a nugget for measurement error;
5. *Simulation* (`vignette("simulation")`): simulation studies, including the recovery of the autocorrelation parameter.

## Growth models

The growth models are curves $f(t)$ that increase from 0, or from the intercept $b_4$ for the Chapman-Richards and Korf curves, towards the asymptote $b_1$. The logistic, Gompertz, Hill, Weibull, beta, normal and gamma curves are sigmoid growth curves, often used in agronomy and ecology; the Chapman-Richards and Korf curves are height-diameter models, common in forestry; and the Preece-Baines curve is a model of human growth in height. The explanatory variable $t$ is usually time, but can be any variable along which the response grows towards an asymptote, e.g. the diameter of trees in a height-diameter model:

| Model | $f(t)$ | $b_2$ | $b_3$ |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| logistic | $b_1 / (1 + \exp(-(t - b_2)/b_3))$ | inflection point, half the asymptote | scale |
| gompertz | $b_1 \exp(-\exp(-(t - b_2)/b_3))$ | inflection point | scale |
| hill | $b_1 / (1 + (b_2/t)^{b_3})$ | half the asymptote | slope on the log time axis |
| weibull | $b_1 (1 - \exp(-\frac{b_3 - 1}{b_3} (t/b_2)^{b_3}))$ | inflection point | shape |
| beta | $b_1 (1 + \frac{b_3 - t}{b_3 - b_2}) (\frac{t - b_4}{b_3 - b_4})^{(b_3 - b_4)/(b_3 - b_2)}$, zero again at $2 b_3 - b_2$ | inflection point | end of growth |
| beta_capped | the same up to $b_3$, and $b_1$ from $b_3$ on | inflection point | end of growth |
| normal | $b_1 \Phi((t - b_2)/b_3)$ | inflection point, half the asymptote | scale |
| gamma | $b_1 F_\Gamma(t;\ b_3, b_2/(b_3 - 1))$ | inflection point | shape |
| chapmanrichards | $b_4 + b_1 (1 - \exp(-b_2 t))^{b_3}$ | rate | shape |
| korf | $b_4 + b_1 \exp(b_2/((1 - b_3) t^{b_3 - 1}))$ | coefficient, $> 0$ | shape, $> 1$ |
| preecebaines | $b_1 - \frac{2 (b_1 - b_3)}{\exp(b_4 (t - b_2)) + \exp(b_5 (t - b_2))}$ | middle of puberty | height at $b_2$ |
| linear | $b_1 t + b_2$ | intercept | not used |

The threshold $b_4$ and the asymmetry $b_5$, the links of the parameters, and the inflection points and maximum growth rates of the models are described in the vignette *Growth models and their parameters*.

## Fitting a growth curve

The examples use the faba bean heights of `FabaHeights26` (see `?FabaHeights26`). `gcTMB()` takes the response and the time in the formula and the growth model in `model`; starting values are found automatically (`gcTMBstart()`).

```{r}
library(gcTMB)
library(ggplot2)
fit <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data = FabaHeights26, model = "logistic")
summary(fit)
```

The growth models are compared by information criteria, e.g. AIC or the criteria of `criteria()`:

```{r}
fits <- lapply(c(logistic = "logistic", gompertz = "gompertz", hill = "hill", weibull = "weibull",
                 beta = "beta", beta_capped = "beta_capped", normal = "normal", gamma = "gamma",
                 chapmanrichards = "chapmanrichards", korf = "korf", preecebaines = "preecebaines",
                 linear = "linear"),
               # the forestry curves from zero at sowing, instead of their default breast height of 1.3
               function(m) gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data = FabaHeights26, model = m,
                                 start = if (m %in% c("chapmanrichards", "korf")) c(b4 = 0)))
criteria(fits, which = c("AIC", "BIC"))
```

`predict()` gives confidence intervals of the mean by the delta method and prediction intervals of new observations; `confint()` gives profile likelihood (default), Wald or parametric bootstrap intervals of the parameters, and `bootstrap()` a bootstrap sample to reuse. `plot()` draws validation plots of the residuals and the fitted curves.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
nd <- data.frame(DAS = seq(0, 125, by = 0.5))
ci <- cbind(nd, predict(fit, newdata = nd, interval = "confidence"))
pi <- cbind(nd, predict(fit, newdata = nd, interval = "prediction"))
ggplot(FabaHeights26, aes(x = DAS, y = Height)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = pi, aes(x = DAS, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "red", alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", size = 0.6, position = position_jitter(width = 0.5, height = 0)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = ci, aes(x = DAS, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "red", alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = ci, aes(y = fit), colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Days after sowing", y = "Height (cm)",
       title = "Logistic curve with 95% confidence (dark) and prediction (light) intervals") +
  theme_minimal()
confint(fit, method = "wald")
```

## Other explanatory variables

The x-axis need not be time: in a height-diameter model of `PineHeightDiameter`, the height grows with the diameter, from the breast height of 1.3 m, the intercept $b_4$ of the Chapman-Richards curve:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
fithd <- gcTMB(Height ~ DBH, rform = b1 ~ 1 | Plot, data = PineHeightDiameter,
               model = "chapmanrichards", start = c(b4 = 1.3))
nd <- data.frame(DBH = seq(0, 52, by = 0.5))
ggplot(PineHeightDiameter, aes(x = DBH, y = Height)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = cbind(nd, Height = predict(fithd, newdata = nd, random = FALSE)), colour = "blue") +
  labs(x = "Diameter at breast height (cm)", y = "Height (m)",
       title = "Scots pines: Chapman-Richards curve from breast height") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Fixed and random effects

Covariates on the parameters are formulas in `fform`, and random effects in `rform`. Here the soil type and the irrigation, and their interaction, act on the asymptote $b_1$ and the time of the maximum growth rate $b_2$, and each plant has correlated random effects on both:

```{r}
fitre <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Soil * Treatment, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | Plant_ID,
               data = FabaHeights26)
fitre
trts <- expand.grid(Soil = c("Loamy", "Sandy"), Treatment = c("Irrigated", "NotIrrigated"))
```

`anova()` gives likelihood ratio tests of nested models, for the fixed effects and for the random effects; `test = "boot"` a parametric bootstrap test, and `test = "F"` F-tests for models without random effects.

```{r}
fitre0 <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Soil + Treatment, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | Plant_ID,
                data = FabaHeights26)
anova(fitre0, fitre)
```

`plot(type = "curves")` draws the curves of the plants and the population curves of the treatments:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
p <- plot(fitre, type = "curves", times = seq(0, 125, by = 0.5), draw = FALSE)
p$curves + labs(x = "Days after sowing", y = "Height (cm)", colour = "Soil, irrigation",
                title = "Curve of each plant (thin) and of each treatment (thick)")
```

`fixef()`, `ranef()` and `VarCorr()` extract the fixed effects, the predicted random effects and their covariance matrices. Random effects can have several terms, nested or crossed grouping factors, and random slopes; see the vignette *Fixed and random effects*.

## Count data and other distributions

The `family` argument gives the distribution of the response: "gaussian", "lognormal", "poisson", "nbinom2", "nbinom1", "binomial", "betabinomial" or "beta". The pods of `FabaCounts23` are zero at the first counts, so the threshold $b_4$, the time of the first pods, is estimated.

```{r}
fitp <- gcTMB(Pods ~ DAS, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Genotype, rform = b1 ~ 1 | Tube_ID, data = FabaCounts23,
              family = "poisson", fix = c(b4 = FALSE))
genotypes <- data.frame(Genotype = sort(unique(FabaCounts23$Genotype)))
cbind(genotypes, predict(fitp, newdata = genotypes, type = "parameters", random = FALSE))
```

`plot()` checks a count model with randomised quantile residuals (Dunn and Smyth, 1996), which are standard normal under the model. The simulations of `simulate()` can also be used for simulation-based residuals, e.g. with the package DHARMa; see the vignette *Fixed and random effects*.

## Timing and maximum growth rates

`timeto()` gives the times at which the curves reach a percentage of their asymptote (or a given response, `type = "absolute"`), and `maxrate()` the maximum growth rate, its timing and the fraction of the asymptote reached then, with standard errors by automatic differentiation and the delta method, and confidence intervals by `confint()`:

```{r}
timeto(fitre, level = 90, newdata = trts, random = FALSE)
maxrate(fitre, newdata = trts)
```

With `b1type = "rate"`, $b_1$ is the maximum growth rate, so that covariates on $b_1$ are effects on the maximum growth rate: `anova()` tests whether they differ, and `partest()` with `contrasts = "tukey"` compares all pairs of genotypes, by Tukey's method with simultaneous confidence intervals.

```{r}
fitpr <- gcTMB(Pods ~ DAS, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Genotype, rform = b1 ~ 1 | Tube_ID, data = FabaCounts23,
               family = "poisson", fix = c(b4 = FALSE), b1type = "rate", link = c(b1 = "log"))
partest(fitpr, newdata = genotypes, contrasts = "tukey")
```

## Correlation structures

The residuals of the gaussian and lognormal families can be correlated within individuals. Over time, `corAR1()` for integer times and `corCAR1()` for continuous times have the correlation $\rho^{|t - s|}$ of residuals at times $s$ and $t$.

```{r}
fitrec <- update(fitre, correlation = corCAR1(value = 0.9, form = ~ DAS | Plant_ID))
corpars(fitrec)
anova(fitre, fitrec)
```

In space, `corExp()` and `corGaus()` have the correlation $(1 - n) \exp(-d/r)$ and $(1 - n) \exp(-(d/r)^2)$ of residuals a distance $d$ apart, with a range $r$ and, with `nugget = TRUE`, a nugget $n$: the share of the residual variance that is independent between observations, such as measurement error. With the positions of trees in their plots, e.g. `corExp(form = ~ X + Y | Plot, nugget = TRUE)`, the residuals of neighbouring trees are correlated. `residuals(type = "normalized")` gives residuals that are independent under the model. The vignette *Correlation structures* describes the models and their likelihood, with an example of spatial correlation.

## Simulation

`simulate()` draws new responses from a fitted model, at the observed times or for new times and individuals in `newdata`, with new random effects and autocorrelated residuals; `update()` sets the parameters of a true model. Refitting the model to simulated data recovers its parameters, e.g. the autocorrelation:

```{r}
design <- expand.grid(DAS = seq(28, 122, by = 7), Plant_ID = paste0("p", 1:30), Soil = "Loamy",
                      Treatment = "Irrigated")
design$Height <- simulate(fitrec, nsim = 1, seed = 1, newdata = design)[[1]]
fitsim <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | Plant_ID, data = design,
                correlation = corCAR1(value = 0.9, form = ~ DAS | Plant_ID))
c(true = corpars(fitrec), estimate = corpars(fitsim))
```

The vignette *Simulation* repeats this for many data sets.

## Convergence

`converged()` checks that the log-likelihood is finite, that the optimiser reports convergence with a largest absolute gradient below $10^{-3}$, and that the Hessian is positive definite. With few groups and several correlated random effects, the likelihood is often so flat in some directions that `nlminb` reports "singular convergence" or "false convergence", or stops with a gradient slightly above $10^{-3}$, although it is at the maximum. With `control = list(restart = TRUE)`, such a fit is optimised once more from its estimates; the fit keeps the better optimum, and `fit$restart$improvement` holds the improvement of the log-likelihood. `converged()` accepts a fit that the restart improved by less than `lltol` ($10^{-6}$ by default), since its maximum is stable. In a simulation study that does not need standard errors, `sdreport = FALSE` saves about a quarter of the time of each fit, but then the Hessian is not checked. The other vignettes use `restart = TRUE` for the fits with several random effects.

## References

Dunn, P.K. and Smyth, G.K. (1996). Randomized quantile residuals. *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics* 5, 236--244. doi:10.1080/10618600.1996.10474708.
